title: Design and Benchmarking of a Quantum Photonic Chip
authors: Gabriele De Angelis, Nicolò Leone, Alessandro Luongo, Alberto Montanaro, Matteo Sanna, Roberto Siagri, Vito Sorianello, Luigi Tallone, Fabrizio Tamburini, Marco Venere
abstract: We present the design and benchmarking of RP000, a quantum photonic processor capable of encoding a quantum system in the degrees of freedom of single photons, based on standard CMOS-compatible manufacturing processes, and working at room temperature. We benchmark it against machine learning tasks, evaluating three quantum-classical architectures of increasing complexity. Our experimental results and simulations show that RP000 achieves higher accuracy than classical networks of comparable size in multiple use cases. Compared to a superconducting quantum processor, RP000 exhibits superior noise tolerance. These findings demonstrate that RP000 can provide a scalable route toward efficient quantum applications.
summary: The paper details the design and rigorous benchmarking of RP000, a silicon-based photonic quantum chip. By applying it to machine learning tasks using hybrid quantum-classical models, the authors demonstrated that the platform achieves high accuracy while showing superior noise resilience compared to superconducting alternatives. This establishes a scalable pathway for efficient quantum computation.
main_problem: The authors designed and benchmarked a room-temperature quantum photonic processor to demonstrate its viability for quantum machine learning tasks.
main_result: The photonic chip achieved higher accuracy than classical networks of comparable size and exhibited superior noise tolerance compared to superconducting processors in benchmarking tests.
method: They implemented various hybrid quantum-classical architectures (SerialQC, ParallelQC) on the hardware platform and benchmarked them against theoretical simulations and superconducting devices using ML datasets.
model_or_system: The system is RP000, a three-qubit photonic processor built on CMOS-compatible silicon photonics. It encodes quantum information in single-photon degrees of freedom and operates via Parametric Quantum Circuits (PQCs).
key_observables: Test accuracy for classification tasks (e.g., STATLOG, YEAST), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) when comparing chip results to theory.
important_parameters: The system uses a $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^3$-graded Lie algebra structure; key hyperparameters tuned include the number of classical components ($N_C$) and encoding strategy ($	ext{ES}$).
main_assumptions: The comparison assumes that statevector tomography can be performed on hardware, and superconducting comparisons used matched sampling statistics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the layered Ansatz circuit structure (Fig. 1) and detail the entire quantum ML training pipeline involving PCA, encoding, and optimization (Fig. 2).
paper_structure: The paper follows a progression from hardware design/calibration to implementing hybrid QML models (QuantumNN $ightarrow$ SerialQC $ightarrow$ ParallelQC), culminating in comprehensive benchmarking against classical and superconducting baselines.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete experimental evidence for scalable, room-temperature quantum computation using photonics, directly addressing the engineering challenges of building practical quantum hardware.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The Ansatz implemented by RP000 which we consider in our experiments. It consists of a layered architecture, where a series of Ry and Rz rotations alternate and CNOT gates generate entanglement.

Fig. 2: Description of the training pipeline for our quantum Ansatz. First, data is pre-processed via PCA; then, the ex- tracted NC components are combined with trainable param- eters via an encoding strategy ES, to produce Nθ rotation angles that feed the Ansatz. The expectation values of the 3 Pauli Z measurement operators will determine our quantum embedding of data. After the labels are derived, we evaluate the considered angles and invoke the Adam optimizer.

Fig. 3: Description of the hybrid models considered by our experimental analysis, integrating a quantum Ansatz into a more extended neural network. The quantum embedding is fed as input to a classical neural network, to provide higher capabilities in feature extraction and class separation in the embedding space.
Fig. 4: Comparison between the frequencies of the value of the sigmoids obtained by the numerical simulation (Theory) and the quantum chip (RP000) for the test set of YEAST.
